1:
The chapter opens on the accession of Ahaz, and the witnesses set his short reign under a shadow from the first line. The reformed John Gill notes only that Ahaz was twenty years old when he began to reign, the verse standing much as it does in the parallel record at 2 Kings 16:2, and turns the reader to the fuller account there. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the same bare notice as the doorway to a whole biography of apostasy: Ahaz succeeds his father Jotham and reigns wickedly for sixteen years, restoring idolatry in its grossest forms, delivered into the hands of Syria and of Israel, plundered by Edom and by the Philistines, and at last spoiling and shutting up the house of God; for the tangled chronology of the accession he simply refers the reader to the difficulties he had weighed at 2 Kings 16:2.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes both the text and the name. The verse is identical with 2 Kings 16:2, though the Septuagint, Syriac, and Arabic read "twenty and five" rather than twenty — a variant that eases a real difficulty, since Hezekiah his son was twenty-five at his own accession, as 2 Chronicles 29:1 records, and a father of thirty-six could scarcely have left a son of that age. Ellicott adds that the Assyrian monuments call Ahaz Yahuhazi, that is Jehoahaz, of which "Ahaz" may be a familiar abridgment, as Jonathan is shortened to Nathan.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the moral frame that the annalist's dry formula implies, naming this plainly the wicked reign of Ahaz in Judah. What the chapter will unfold, Henry sees, is the settled law of such a life: when sinners are left to their own hearts' lusts they grow more desperate in wickedness, and the progress of wickedness and misery is often rapid. It is an awful thing, he warns, to reflect upon a sinner being driven away in his wickedness into the eternal world — the very end toward which this reign is already hastening from its opening verse.

The witnesses do not divide over substance. Gill and Ellicott secure the text and its variant; Clarke lays out the arc of the reign in a breath; Henry sounds the note the whole chapter will carry. Whether Ahaz was twenty or twenty-five at his crowning, all agree that he came to the throne of David a grown and responsible man, old enough to know the God he would forsake, and that the story now to be told is not of a king misled by others but of one who chose, deliberately and with open eyes, the way of ruin.
2:
With the accession noted, the witnesses turn to the substance of Ahaz's guilt, and the grammatical-historical voices carry the verse almost alone. Keil and Delitzsch read the opening clause as the master-charge of the whole reign: Ahaz walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, taking up the state religion of the northern kingdom, and beyond even that he made molten images for the Baalim. The plural is deliberate — not a single idol but a whole apparatus of them, so that the apostasy of Ahaz outran the calf-worship of the north and reached into the grosser Canaanite cults his fathers had refused.

Charles Ellicott presses the same phrase. "For the Baals," he renders it — the different aspects or avatars of the Canaanite god, worshipped under their several names. This clause, he observes, is the chronicler's own addition, set down to explain the more general charge that Ahaz walked in the way of the kings of Israel; for that way was precisely the state recognition of Baal-worship side by side with the worship of Jehovah, the syncretism that had entered the house of David through its marriage-alliance with the house of Ahab, as the earlier reigns at 2 Chronicles 21:6 and 2 Chronicles 22:3 had already shown. Ellicott suggests that both this clause and the opening words of the next verse may have fallen out of the parallel text of Kings, so that the chronicler here preserves what the older record lost.

The two witnesses do not divide; they build one portrait. Where a king merely tolerant of the calves might be charged with weakness, Ahaz is charged with invention — casting new gods with his own hand, multiplying the objects of a false devotion. Keil and Delitzsch weigh the word "molten" as marking images deliberately manufactured, and Ellicott weighs the plural "Baalim" as marking a cult of many faces; between them they show that Ahaz did not drift into idolatry but engineered it. The formula "he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel" will return like a refrain across the chapter, and here at its first sounding the witnesses fix its meaning: it names not a lapse of policy but a wholesale importing into Judah of the very apostasy that was even then dragging the northern kingdom to its grave. The king of David's line has set himself to out-sin the calf-kings, and the verses that follow will trace, step by step, the judgment that such invention draws down.
3:
The idolatry deepens into atrocity, and the witnesses gather around the valley of the son of Hinnom and the fire in which Ahaz burned his own children. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott identifies the god and the ground: it was to Moloch, the god of Ammon for whom Solomon had built a high place at 1 Kings 11:5 and which still stood, that Ahaz burned incense; and the valley of Hinnom lay west and south of Jerusalem, the scene of the cruel rites named in Jeremiah 7:31. He traces the after-history of the name: in later times "the valley of Hinnom," contracted and revowelled to Ge-hinnom, became the very word for hell, passing through the Targums into the Greek Gehenna of the New Testament. On the burning itself Ellicott is careful. Where Kings says Ahaz "made his son to pass through the fire," the chronicler writes that he "burned" his children — a paraphrase, Ellicott judges, formed by transposing two Hebrew letters; and "his children" is a generalizing plural, one of the marks of the chronicler's style, as at Psalms 106:37, not necessarily a claim that more than one son was offered.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fastens on that very fire and preserves a striking rabbinic tradition. The Targum, he reports, expands the verse with a legend that the Word of the Lord snatched Hezekiah from among the children Ahaz cast into the flames of Tophet, because it was appointed that from him the three faithful confessors — Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah — should one day proceed; and the tradition strings together the great deliverances from fire, from Abram in the Chaldean furnace to the three in the furnace of Babylon. Clarke passes the midrash on for what it is worth, a witness to how deeply the horror of Ahaz's altars burned itself into later memory.

Ellicott notes too that the critic Thenius accused the chronicler of exaggerating the fact by the change from "passing through" to "burning"; but Ellicott answers that the peculiar plural is simply a feature of this writer's manner, not an inflation of the crime. The two witnesses do not contend. Clarke supplies the fire's long shadow in the memory of the synagogue; Ellicott supplies the philology and the geography, and the sober note that this valley of children's ashes would lend its name to the place of final woe. Together they let the verse stand at its full weight: a king of Judah, on the high places and under every green tree and in the smoking gorge below his city, gave his own sons to the flames — the deepest descent of an apostasy that began with molten calves and ends at the mouth of hell.
5:
The judgment falls, and the witnesses read the double defeat as the chronicler's chosen illustration of God chastising an apostate king. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott opens with the very first words, "the LORD his God delivered him," which explain, he says, why this account varies from the parallel: the chronicler purposes not so much to describe a campaign as to select those events that most conspicuously display God's dealings with Ahaz, so that throughout the section the historical is subordinated to the didactic — not history for its own sake, but history teaching by example, as in the earlier Syrian invasion at 2 Chronicles 24:23. The king of Syria is Rezin of Damascus; "smote him" means, literally, smote in his army, that is defeated him; and the great captivity carried off answers to the panic finely painted at Isaiah 7:2. Ellicott adds that the whole passage is above critical suspicion, noting that even Thenius pronounced the section thoroughly historical.

The reformed John Gill lingers over the tender phrase "the LORD his God." God was Ahaz's God of right, having dominion over him and deserving his worship; God was his God by the national covenant made with the people he ruled; and God was his God even by Ahaz's own hypocritical profession, though he had forsaken the true worship. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the same words to the same end: God was his God, not by any special relation, which Ahaz had renounced, but by his sovereign dominion over him — for God did not forfeit his right by Ahaz's denying it. The two agree that the title is no compliment to the king but a rebuke: the very God he betrayed was the God who handed him over.

The other wesleyan-arminian witness, Adam Clarke, is content to refer the reader to the fuller notes on the joint campaign at 2 Kings 16:5, where the confederacy of Rezin and Pekah against Jerusalem is told. The witnesses converge on the chapter's governing logic. Ellicott lays bare the writer's method — two crushing defeats in the open field chosen out of the war to show the hand of God; Gill and Wesley lay bare the writer's theology in a single possessive pronoun. Ahaz is not overthrown by the mere fortune of arms but delivered up, and delivered up by the very LORD whose he was and whom he had cast off. The syncretist who cast molten Baals finds that the God of Israel is no idol to be juggled, but a living Lord who gives his own rebellious king into the hand of the enemy.
6:
The scale of the slaughter draws the witnesses at once to the number and to its cause. The reformed John Gill identifies the agent — Pekah the son of Remaliah, at this time king of Israel — and lets the figure stand. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch ground the carnage in the verse's own reason: a hundred and twenty thousand valiant men fell in Judah in one day because they had forsaken the LORD God of their fathers; the sin of the king had become the sin of the people, and the sword reaped what the apostasy had sown.

Charles Ellicott measures the number against the muster-rolls. "In one day" means in one great engagement, the Hebrew often using "day" for a day of battle; and if the figure is exact, some third of the Jewish host counted at 2 Chronicles 26:13 had fallen in the battle and pursuit. The ruthlessness is confirmed, he notes, by Oded's own words in the next verses about a rage that reaches to heaven, and by the allies' design, disclosed at Isaiah 7:6, to break the independence of Judah altogether and set up a puppet in David's room. The people fell, he adds with the chronicler, because they had forsaken, echoing the charge at 2 Chronicles 27:2.

Here the witnesses divide. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds the number scarcely credible: it is hardly possible, he says, that a hundred and twenty thousand men could be slain in a single day, though he owns that all the versions and manuscripts agree in it, and supposes the whole people were given up into their enemies' hands. Keil and Delitzsch answer the objection head-on: the modern critics — Gesenius, De Wette, Winer — took offense at these figures and pronounced them the exaggerations of a wonder-loving chronicler, but in this they are mistaken, for the aim of the allies, as Isaiah 7:6 shows, was the annihilation of the kingdom, and the Ephraimites always waged war with extreme cruelty. So the debate is real: is the vast total a copyist's swelling of the record, or the sober measure of a war meant to end the house of David?

The other wesleyan-arminian voice, John Wesley, presses the poetic justice beneath the horror. Ahaz had walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, and God chose the king of Israel for his scourge: it is just with God, Wesley says, to make them a plague to us whom we have made our patterns, or our partners, in sin. The sword that fell on Judah was wielded by the very apostasy Ahaz had courted. The witnesses agree, whatever their reckoning of the number, that the day's catastrophe was no accident of arms but the LORD's own answer to a people who had forsaken him.
7:
The battle claims three men close to the throne, and the witnesses read the verse as the war striking at the very household of Ahaz. The reformed John Gill names the first casualty, Maaseiah the king's son, cut down by Zichri, a mighty man of Ephraim — a prince who must therefore have escaped the fires of the valley of Hinnom, or only been made to pass through them, since the same king who slew his children in the flame now loses a kinsman to the Ephraimite sword.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the rank of the three fallen. Keil and Delitzsch judge that Maaseiah cannot be a literal son of Ahaz, for in the first years of the reign, when this war fell, the king can have had no son grown enough to bear arms; he is rather a royal prince, a cousin or an uncle, as the phrase "the king's son" is used at 2 Chronicles 18:25. Azrikam they take to be governor of the palace, a high officer of the royal house; and Elkanah, "next to the king," to be his first minister, his grand vizier, as the like title stands at Esther 10:3. Charles Ellicott reads the three names in the same way and gives the reason the chronicler troubled to record them: he mentions these deaths precisely because of the men's intimate connection with Ahaz, whose punishment he is describing, for the blow that struck them struck the king, as the like slaughter of royal kinsmen had done at 2 Chronicles 24:23.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill supplies the grim link back to the valley of fire; Keil and Ellicott settle the offices and the relationships, and both agree on the point that matters to the narrative. This is no random tally of the dead but a deliberate reckoning: a prince of the blood, the steward of the palace, and the chief minister of state all fell together in a single day, so that the throne of Ahaz was left stripped of its nearest supports. The chronicler counts them one by one because each was a limb of the royal house, and their common fall is the measure of how deep the judgment cut. The king who had given his own children to Moloch now sees the men nearest his own person given to the sword; the ruin he had courted for Judah has reached his very door.
8:
Two hundred thousand of Judah are led away captive, and the witnesses weigh both the barbarity of the deed and the credibility of the count. The reformed John Gill marks the number as very large and unusual, and explains how it was done: the men having been slaughtered in such multitudes, the rest were the more easily overpowered, so that women and children by the myriad were swept off to Samaria. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fasten on the word the chronicler chooses, "their brethren" — a term set down with emphasis, here and again in the appeal that follows, to expose the cruelty of Israelites who did not scruple to carry into slavery the defenseless women and children of their own kin.

Keil and Delitzsch turn at once to the critics who stumble at the figures. The modern scholars — Gesenius, De Wette, Winer — have taken offense at a hundred and twenty thousand slain and two hundred thousand led away, and declared them the exaggerations of a wonder-loving chronicler; but, they insist, this is a mistake, for a closer look at the war, and at the design disclosed in Isaiah 7:6 to make an end of the kingdom of Judah, shows the numbers to answer to the fury of the assault, and the Ephraimites were always cruel in war.

Charles Ellicott brings the decisive external witness. The phrase "of their brethren," he agrees, heightens the barbarity of the deed; and then he sets beside the chronicler's total a foreign and wholly unrelated record: Sennacherib boasts on his own monuments that in the later war against Hezekiah he took forty-six strong cities of Judah and carried off two hundred thousand one hundred and fifty captives. The number of the text, Ellicott concludes, is thus corroborated from a source that had no interest in confirming it — a striking answer to the charge of exaggeration. He notes too that the thrilling narrative of Kings, its eye fixed on Jerusalem, says nothing of that Assyrian deportation, just as the parallel to this section is silent about the captives of Ahaz's day.

The witnesses do not divide; they close ranks against the critics. Gill fixes the sad arithmetic, Keil defends it by the temper of the war, and Ellicott clinches it by the boast of a heathen conqueror who carried off almost the identical number a generation later. What none of them lets slip is the word that governs the verse. These were "brethren" — bone of the same bone, children of the one covenant — and to drive them in chains to Samaria was to turn a chastisement of Judah into a crime of Israel, a crime the prophet Oded is even now hastening out of the city to arrest.
9:
At the gate of Samaria a prophet steps into the path of the triumphant army, and the witnesses gather around Oded with unusual warmth. The reformed John Gill fixes his identity, distinguishing him from the earlier Oded of Asa's day. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe him as a prophet of the true God — not of the calf-Jahve worshipped in the images, but of the living LORD, a labourer in the northern kingdom like the prophet Hosea — who went out to meet the returning host as Azariah once met Asa at 2 Chronicles 15:2, laid bare the cruelty of their treatment of their brethren, and pressed them to turn away the wrath they had incurred by sending the captives home.

Charles Ellicott sharpens the prophet's argument to its edge. "In the wrath of Jehovah against Judah he gave them into your hand" — the victory, that is, was due to God's punitive anger, not to Israel's valour or intrinsic worth; they ought to have weighed this and shown compassion to the victims of the divine displeasure, but instead they had given full rein to a furious hatred. The rage that "reaches up to heaven," he explains, is a guilty excess that calls to heaven for vengeance, like the blood of Abel crying from the ground at Genesis 4:10. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the phrase the same way — an unbounded rage, which cries to God for vengeance against such bloody men — while Adam Clarke, of the same school, can scarcely praise the speech enough: simple, humane, pious, and overwhelmingly convincing, it produced the very effect it sought, and proves how much humanity still lodged in the chiefs of Ephraim who joined the prophet's plea.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the moral the prophet drives home. Israel gained the victory only because God was wroth with Judah and made them the rod of his indignation; and now Oded reminds them of their own sins, that they may see how ill it becomes sinners to be cruel. Could they hope for the mercy of God, Henry asks, if they showed neither mercy nor justice to their brethren? Ellicott adds the historian's curiosity that neither this narrative nor its parallel names the great prophet Hosea, who must then have been at work in the north; but of Oded nothing further is known. The witnesses do not divide. They agree that the sermon at the city gate is the hinge of the chapter: a word of God, spoken in the enemy's own capital, that turns a column of chained captives back toward home, and teaches conqueror and reader alike that a victory granted in wrath confers no licence to be cruel.
10:
Oded turns from the slaughter to the slavery the victors intend, and the witnesses read the verse as both a legal indictment and a searching question. The reformed John Gill states the charge plainly: the men of Israel now purpose to keep the children of Judah and Jerusalem under them as bondmen and bondwomen, a design flatly contrary to the law. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the emphatic Hebrew, in which "the sons of Judah" stand first for stress — your very brethren, whom the wrath of God has smitten, these you propose to hold in subjection — and then the doubled "you, even you" that turns the accusation back on the accusers: are there not, with you yourselves, sins against the LORD your God? Charles Ellicott renders the abrupt question the same way: are you the only guiltless people, that your indignation should burn so hot against your brethren? The reference, he suggests, is to the calves of Bethel and Dan — Israel's own standing apostasy, which left them in no position to play the avenging judge.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry seizes the moment for its widest lesson. It ill becomes sinners to be cruel; and here he presses the point into a principle that reaches far beyond the day: no man acquainted with the word of God, he says, need fear to maintain that slavery is against the law of love and the gospel of grace. Who can hold his brother in bondage without breaking the rule of doing to others as he would they should do to him, the golden rule of Matthew 7:12? Every man, Henry insists, is our neighbour, our brother, our fellow-man, if not our fellow-Christian; and to reduce such a one to a chattel is to trample the very charity the prophet is pleading.

The witnesses do not divide; they lay the same weight from three directions. Gill names the breach of the law, Keil and Ellicott expose the hypocrisy of guilty men presuming to enslave their guilty brethren, and Henry lifts the particular case into the abiding truth that bondage of a brother offends the law of love itself. Oded's question hangs unanswered in the verse — are there no trespasses with you? — and its force is that the sword of judgment which had fallen on Judah could as justly fall on Samaria, whose calves still stood. The would-be slaveholders are themselves under wrath; and the only escape the prophet will allow them is not to bind their brethren but to loose them.
11:
The prophet's argument becomes a command, and the witnesses attend to the note of urgency in it. The reformed John Gill catches the double demand in "now hear me therefore" — not merely to hear but to obey; the word calls for action, not attention only. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the ground of the charge: having quickened their conscience, Oded now bids them send back the prisoners they had carried off from among their brethren, because the fierce wrath of Jahve was upon them. Already in the pitiless butchery of their kinsmen they had committed a sin that cried to heaven and challenged God's anger; but by dragging away the women and children they had filled up the measure of their guilt, so that unless they relented the wrath and rage of God must fall upon Israel itself.

Charles Ellicott adds the two small precisions of grammar and of law. The "and now" that opens the verse is illative, not temporal — a "therefore" drawing the conclusion from all that has gone before, rather than a mere mark of time. And the demand rests on more than sentiment: Leviticus 25:39 expressly forbids the permanent enslaving of Israelite by Israelite, so that in proposing to keep their brethren as bondmen the victors were setting themselves squarely against the Mosaic statute. The prophet is not pleading a private tenderness but recalling a plain command of God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry marks the outcome the verse sets in motion: God commands them to release the prisoners, and they obeyed. It is the rare and beautiful moment when a word of rebuke is met not with resentment but with repentance. The witnesses do not divide. Gill hears the imperative in "hear me," Keil measures the wrath that hangs over an unrelenting Israel, Ellicott anchors the demand in the written law, and Henry records the glad end — obedience. Together they show the prophet closing his appeal with the only motive that could move armed and victorious men: not that mercy is becoming, though he had urged that, but that the same LORD whose wrath had just crushed Judah stood ready to turn that wrath on Israel next, and that the one way to escape it was to open the captives' chains. Judgment and mercy meet in the command; the sword that fell on the one kingdom is held over the other, and the prophet offers deliverance from it at the price of setting the prisoners free.
12:
The prophet's word finds allies among the leaders of the people, and the witnesses trace how the appeal turned into action. The reformed John Gill notes only that certain of the heads of the children of Ephraim — the principal men of the ten tribes — now come forward, and lets their names follow. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch record the depth of the impression Oded's speech had made: four of the Ephraimite chiefs, named here one by one, stood at the head of the assembled people and came out to meet those returning from the war, the idiom for placing oneself in another's path to withstand him. They are the men who will speak in the next verse, refusing to let the captives be brought in.

Charles Ellicott attends to the political sense of the title and the exact force of the verb. "The children of Ephraim," he explains, is the standing name by which the prophets of that age — Hosea and Isaiah among them — designate the ten tribes as a single political whole, Ephraim being the leading tribe of the north. And the Hebrew phrase rendered "stood up against" commonly means to oppose; here it bears the sense of confronting or coming before those who were arriving from the host — not a hostile onset but a resolute interposition, planting themselves in the road to bar the captives' entry.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill points to the princes, Keil counts and places them at the head of the congregation, and Ellicott secures both the collective name and the exact colour of the verb. What all three quietly register is a thing rare in the annals of a conquering army: that when a prophet of God rebuked the victors in their own capital, it was the leading men of the nation, and not a faction of the defeated, who rose to enforce his word. The four named chiefs make themselves a living barrier between the returning soldiers and the gate of Samaria, and their stand gives the prophet's plea its teeth. Oded had supplied the conscience; these princes supply the authority; and between the man of God and the heads of the people the tide of a whole army is about to be turned. The verse is the pivot on which the mercy of the chapter swings from word to deed, and the chronicler names the four, as he named the fallen officers of Ahaz, because their act deserved to be remembered.
13:
The princes speak, and the witnesses read their protest as a confession as much as a command. The reformed John Gill sets the scene: "ye shall not bring in the captives hither" means not into Samaria, near which the army now was, the chiefs forbidding the prisoners the very gate of the city. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the heart of the speech: bring not the captives here, for you purpose to add to our sins and to our guilt, seeing a trespass against Jahve already lies upon us; great is our guilt, and fierce wrath is upon Israel already. The princes do not plead their own innocence; they plead the opposite — that the nation is already so laden with sin and so exposed to wrath that it dare not pile the enslaving of brethren upon the heap.

Charles Ellicott weighs the disputed grammar of the opening clause and comes to the same sense. The words may be rendered "whereas we have offended against the LORD already," or, as some prefer, "so that a trespass against Jehovah come upon us"; but either way, he observes, the elders openly admit an existing trespass when they add, "for our trespass is great, and there is fierce wrath against Israel." What they deprecate is not a guilt they deny but an aggravation of the guilt they own. Ellicott notes too the marks of the passage's transmission — that the Syriac takes a shorter road through these verses — a reminder of how carefully the record was handed down.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the place, Keil and Ellicott fix the plea, and all three catch the remarkable temper of it. Here are the leaders of a victorious army confessing, in the flush of triumph, that their own account with God stands badly overdrawn, and refusing on that very ground to wrong their brethren further. It is repentance reasoning about consequences: men who have seen the sword of God fall on Judah for its sin, and who know their own sin to be no less, and who therefore will not court the same stroke by adding cruelty to apostasy. The captives shall not enter the city, not because the victors have suddenly grown tender, but because they have grown afraid — afraid of a wrath already kindled, which one more trespass might turn full upon Samaria. The confession of guilt becomes, in the princes' mouths, the shield of the oppressed.
14:
The soldiers yield, and the witnesses pause over the plain wonder of an army laying down its plunder at a word. The reformed John Gill records the scene simply: the armed men left the captives and the spoil before the princes and the congregation who had come out from Samaria to meet them; such was the effect of the prophet's word and the princes' stand that the soldiers surrendered not only the prisoners but the booty too, for the leaders to dispose of as they saw fit. Charles Ellicott of the grammatical-historical school fixes the actors: the "armed men" are the returning host, the "princes" are the four heads named just before, and "the congregation" is the assembly of the citizens gathered at the gate of Samaria — the whole city, in effect, standing witness to the release.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the moral hidden in the surrender. In leaving the captives, he says, the soldiers showed a more truly heroic bravery than they had shown in taking them; for it is true honour for a man to yield to reason and religion even in spite of his own interest. The victors gave up the fruit of their victory — the ransom, the slaves, the spoil that was theirs by the hard law of war — and Wesley counts that renunciation the greater conquest. To master an enemy is the work of an hour and an army; to master oneself, to loose one's grip on lawful gain at the bidding of conscience, is the rarer valour.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott set the fact and name the parties; Wesley supplies its praise. Between them they mark the turning of the whole episode: the column of chained brethren, which a moment before was being driven into bondage, now stands free before the assembly, and the spoil beside it, waiting to be turned to their relief. It is a scene the chronicler plainly means his readers to admire — hardened fighting men, flushed with a great victory, halting at the word of a single prophet and the resolve of four princes, and quietly setting down what they had every worldly right to keep. The next verse will show what that surrendered spoil was used for; here the wonder is only that it was surrendered at all, and Wesley's verdict stands over it: to yield thus is the truest bravery of the two.
15:
The chapter reaches its height of tenderness as the captives are not merely freed but cherished, and the witnesses linger over each act of mercy. The reformed John Gill takes "the men that were expressed by name" to be either those chiefs just named or others specially appointed, who now rose up to the work. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch prefer to read them as men marked out by name for distinction — prominent men, the four princes among them but not they alone — who received the prisoners and the booty, and out of that very spoil clothed all the naked among them, gave them food and drink, anointed them, set the feeble upon asses, and brought them to Jericho, the city of palm trees, to their brethren, before returning to Samaria. The picture, they say, is drawn with evident satisfaction, portraying the loving pity of the strong for the miserable.

Charles Ellicott dwells on the same details and reads them for their echoes. The captives were clothed and shod out of the plunder, as the wretched destitution of prisoners required; they were anointed, the ordinary kindness of that climate, the word the same used of the woman at Luke 7:38; and the feeble, being mostly women and children, were mounted on asses for the long road down to Jericho. The writer dwells with manifest pleasure, Ellicott notes, on this kindness of repentant foes, and may have meant it as a rebuke to the bitter Samaritans of his own day, who so harried the returned exiles at Nehemiah 4:2. He records the old suggestion that our Lord had this very passage in mind when he framed the parable of the good Samaritan at Luke 10:30, so close are the coincidences of clothing, healing oil, the beast, and the journey; and he sets the prophet Oded's interposition between Ephraim and its captives beside that of Shemaiah between the tribes at 1 Kings 12:22. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds only that the men "expressed by name" were those appointed to manage the business.

The witnesses do not divide; they contemplate the same beautiful thing. Gill and Wesley settle who did the work, Keil paints the compassion, and Ellicott hears in it the anticipation of the gospel's own charity. Out of the spoil of a cruel war the victors clothe and feed and heal the very people they had meant to enslave, and carry the weakest of them home on their own beasts. It is the mercy that the prophet's word had wrung from an army, made visible in bread and sandals and oil; and the chronicler holds it up, across the centuries, as the pattern of what it means to treat an enemy as a brother.
16:
The narrative leaves Samaria's mercy and returns to Ahaz's folly, as the beaten king looks for a rescuer, and the witnesses fix at once on the odd plural "kings of Assyria." The reformed John Gill takes it as a reference to Tiglath-pileser and his son, though he notes that the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic, with the Targum, all read the singular "king." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees the plural is a difficulty: against "kings" the ancient versions, a Hebrew manuscript, and the parallel at 2 Kings 16:7 all have the singular, and the king in question was certainly Tiglath-pileser, as the second book of Kings makes plain. Charles Ellicott of the grammatical-historical school reads it as a generalized expression, like the plural "Baalim" earlier in the chapter, and observes that all the old versions render it "king"; John Wesley of the wesleyan-arminian school smooths it by taking the "kings" to be princes, who might be so styled in a looser use of the word.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, grant the plural is rhetorical but will not let it be flattened away, for they find in it the whole tragedy of the appeal. The plural is of a piece with the plural "Baalim," a form that expresses a thought: that Ahaz, instead of seeking the help of Jahve his God, which the prophet had pressed on him at Isaiah 7:4, turned to the kings of the world-power, the great empire so hostile to the kingdom of God, from whom he could obtain no real help at all. That Ahaz applied in fact to one king only, Keil adds, is clear from the verses that follow.

So the witnesses divide only on the surface. Over the grammar there is a mild debate — whether "kings" is a copyist's plural to be corrected to the singular of the versions, or a rhetorical plural that the writer meant. But beneath it they are one. Every voice knows that a single monarch, Tiglath-pileser, is meant; and Keil draws out what the others leave implicit, that the plural, whatever its origin, points to the direction of Ahaz's heart. Offered the help of the LORD through Isaiah, he spurned it and sent instead to the idol-serving empire of the north, laying the kingdom of David at the feet of the very power that would in time devour it. The verse is the hinge of his ruin: a king delivered up by his God now seeks salvation from the world, and finds, as the next verses will show, that the world exacts far more than it gives.
17:
The reason for Ahaz's desperate embassy begins to appear, as fresh enemies close in from every side, and the witnesses turn first to Edom. The reformed John Gill notes that the Edomites had come again, as they had in the days of Jehoshaphat, and had smitten Judah and carried off captives of their own. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse with its connecting word: "and besides," over and above the Syrian and Ephraimite disasters, the Edomites had come and inflicted a defeat on Judah and led captives away. They recall the history behind the raid: Edom had been subdued and held in vassalage only by Amaziah and Uzziah, as at 2 Chronicles 25:11 and 2 Chronicles 26:2; but once Rezin of Syria had freed them from that yoke, as 2 Kings 16:6 records, they seized the moment to break loose and take their revenge on the people who had oppressed them.

Charles Ellicott reads the verse the same way and fills in the sequence of cause and effect. "And moreover," he renders the opening, and takes "smitten Judah" to mean inflicted a defeat upon her. After their reduction by Uzziah the Edomites had probably remained subject to Judah, he judges, until Rezin expelled the Jews from Elath and restored the port to Syrian and Edomite hands; and after that reverse the mounting disasters of Ahaz emboldened them to make a raid upon his territory. The old subject-people, watching the throne of Judah reel under blow after blow, chose their hour and struck.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill sets the Edomite inroad in the long memory of earlier invasions; Keil and Ellicott trace the political thread — vassalage under Amaziah and Uzziah, release by Rezin, revolt and revenge under Ahaz. What all three register is the gathering completeness of the judgment. It is not one enemy but many; the Syrian from the north, the Ephraimite from the north, and now the Edomite from the south, each falling on Judah in turn as the hand of God is felt withdrawing its hedge. The very nations his stronger fathers had held down now rise against Ahaz, and the kingdom that had oppressed its neighbours in its strength is preyed upon by them in its weakness. The chronicler is building his account, blow upon blow, toward the point of the whole section — that an apostate king, forsaken by the LORD, is left exposed on every frontier, and that his frantic appeal to Assyria is the flailing of a man already sinking.
18:
A second frontier gives way as the Philistines pour into the western lowlands, and the witnesses map the lost towns and the reversal they mark. The reformed John Gill sets the invasion in its motive: the Philistines fell upon the cities of the low country nearest them and pressed on to the south of Judah, taking their revenge for what Uzziah had done to them in his strength. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the point explicit — these were the Philistines whom Uzziah had subdued at 2 Chronicles 26:6, who now used the pressure of the Syrians and Ephraimites upon Judah not only to throw off the yoke but to plunder and to enlarge their own borders. They tell over the captured towns one by one — Bethshemesh, Ajalon, Gederoth, Shocho, which Rehoboam had fortified at 2 Chronicles 11:7, Timnah, and Gimzo with their dependent villages.

Charles Ellicott adds the geography and the grammar. "Invaded" means fell upon; the "low country" is the shephelah, the lowland of Judah between the hills and the Mediterranean, and the "south" is the Negeb, the southland nearly coextensive with the old territory of Simeon. He identifies the sites in turn — Bethshemesh, Ajalon, Gederoth in the lowland, Socho, Timnah, and Gimzo between Lydda and Bethhoron — and takes the closing words "and they dwelt there" to mean that the Philistines did not merely raid but permanently occupied the conquered country, settling in the towns they had seized.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill supplies the motive of revenge, Keil the strategic opportunism and the roll of towns, Ellicott the exact bounds and the note of permanence. Together they measure the shrinking of Judah on its western and southern flanks: fortified cities that a strong king had once wrested from the Philistines or built up against them now pass back into enemy hands, and the enemy stays. The chronicler is completing the circle of the judgment he began with Syria and Ephraim and Edom. The kingdom of Ahaz is being eaten inward from every quarter at once, its borders rolled back, its garrison towns lost, its people carried off; and the reason has been stated once and will be stated again — that the LORD is bringing Judah low. The map of the lost cities is a map of a nation under the withdrawn favour of God, and the next verse will name that withdrawal for what it is.
19:
The chronicler pauses to name the true cause behind every enemy, and the witnesses fasten on his verdict and on the strange title he gives the king. "The LORD brought Judah low because of Ahaz king of Israel": the reformed John Gill takes the cause plainly — it was for the impieties and idolatries of Ahaz, into which the people followed his example, that God humbled them. As for the title, Gill reads it in more than one way: Ahaz is called king of Israel because he walked in the ways of the kings of Israel, and because he ruled over tribes of Israel and was of right their king, as David and Solomon had been; though he notes that several versions and the Targum here read "king of Judah," and that "made Judah naked" means he stripped the people of their religion and so of the divine protection.

The grammatical-historical witnesses press the title harder. Keil and Delitzsch call it ironical: Ahaz is styled king of Israel not because he walked in the northern ways but because his government was the bitterest satire on the very name of Israel, the people of God, so that the word is used in its full pregnant weight. Charles Ellicott sees the same irony but adds the chronicler's habitual usage, in which the southern kingdom is itself the true "Israel," as at 2 Chronicles 21:2; and he reads "made Judah naked" more exactly as "he behaved licentiously, dealt loosely, in Judah," the verb used in this sense here alone, with "transgressed sore" meaning he committed unfaithfulness against the LORD.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the practical lesson from "brought low." They that will not humble themselves under the word of God, he says, will be humbled by his judgments; and "naked" he takes richly — stripped of their ornament and their defence at once: their treasures, sent uselessly to the Assyrian; their frontier towns and strongholds, lost by the king's folly; and above all their religion and the divine protection, which had been their great and only firm security. And the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the seal on it: the LORD brought Judah low, and those who will not humble themselves under the word of God will justly be humbled by his judgments. The witnesses do not divide on the substance. Whether the title be read as literal, or as biting irony, or as the chronicler's pregnant "Israel," all agree on the verse's burden: the armies of Syria, Ephraim, Edom, and Philistia were only rods; the hand that wielded them was God's, and the sin that moved the hand was the king's.
20:
The Assyrian whom Ahaz had bought comes at last, but not as the deliverer the king had hoped, and the witnesses expose the bitter irony of the "help." The reformed John Gill notes that Tiglath-pileser came unto him — not to Jerusalem, but to Damascus, where he made a diversion in Ahaz's favour, took the city, and where Ahaz went to meet him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fills in the campaign from the parallel and the monuments: induced by the message and the present of Ahaz, Tiglath-pileser marched west, captured Damascus, slew Rezin, and carried its people away to Kir, as told at 2 Kings 16:9; afterward Ahaz travelled to Damascus to do him homage, as at 2 Kings 16:10. But the Assyrian came with no purpose of strengthening the southern kingdom. Glad of a pretext for meddling in the west, the ambitious conqueror simply extended his own empire, and when the stronger states of Syria and Israel lay at his feet he required of Ahaz an unmistakable acknowledgment of vassalage. He "distressed" him by reducing Judah to a mere dependency and draining it of all its treasure — a tributary bondage plain from 2 Kings 18:7.

Keil and Delitzsch keep to the pointed antithesis of the verse: the king of Assyria came against him and distressed him, but strengthened him not. The very ally hired to help became a fresh oppressor; the remedy proved another disease.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws out the emphatic contrast with a statesman's eye. "Distressed" he glosses as straitened, by robbing Ahaz of his treasures; and "strengthened not" he calls a most emphatical expression, for though the Assyrian weakened the present enemy, the Syrian, yet, all things considered, he did not strengthen Ahaz and his kingdom but weakened them. By removing the Syrian, who though a troublesome neighbour had served as a kind of bulwark, Tiglath-pileser smoothed his own road toward Judah — a far more dangerous enemy than the one he had cleared away, as the very next reign would prove.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill sets the meeting at Damascus, Ellicott lays out the conqueror's self-interest and the reduction of Judah to a vassal, Keil sharpens the antithesis, and Wesley reads the long-range folly of it. All see the same grim lesson the chronicler is teaching: the king who would not lean on the LORD leaned on Assyria, and Assyria bent him to the ground. He bought a protector and got a master; he spent the treasure of temple and palace to purchase, not deliverance, but the first instalment of a bondage that would one day swallow the kingdom whole.
21:
The price of that empty alliance is now reckoned, and the witnesses count what Ahaz stripped away to pay it. The reformed John Gill itemizes the spoil: Ahaz took a portion out of the treasures of the house of the LORD, a portion out of his own royal treasury, and a further levy raised upon his princes, gathering the costly bribe from temple, palace, and nobility alike. Charles Ellicott of the grammatical-historical school renders the tenses more exactly — "for Ahaz had despoiled the house of the LORD, and the house of the king and of the princes, and had given it" — and identifies "the princes" as the great courtiers of the palace, whose valuables, with the king's, were ransacked to make up the tribute, as the parallel gift is described at 2 Kings 16:8.

On the crowning clause, "but he helped him not," the witnesses are one. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it flatly: the Assyrian did him no ultimate service, and refers to the fuller note at 2 Kings 16:9. Ellicott renders it "it was not for help to him" — the submission to Tiglath-pileser brought no real advantage but rather hastened the kingdom's downfall; and he quotes the judgment that the Assyrians had no regard for the welfare of their vassals, the principle of that monarchy being plunder, so that Ahaz, his treasury once exhausted by the first tribute, would soon be driven to strip the very bronze-work and fixed ornaments from the temple, as 2 Kings 16:17 records, until the day when the Assyrian's rapacity could no longer be satisfied and his hordes would be loosed upon the land.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry supplies the human bitterness beneath the transaction: it is often found, he observes, that wicked men themselves have no real affection for those that revolt to them, nor do they care to do them a kindness. Ahaz had forsaken his God to court a heathen empire, and the empire took his gold and gave him nothing but a heavier yoke. The witnesses do not divide. Gill counts the plundered treasure, Ellicott and Clarke trace the tribute to its worthlessness, Henry names the folly of trusting such an ally. All see the chronicler pressing his lesson home: the king who robbed the house of God to buy the friendship of the world found that the world pockets the bribe and despises the giver. What Ahaz surrendered to Assyria was not the last of his losses but the first, the opening payment of a servitude that no amount of temple-gold could ever buy off.
22:
Affliction, which softens some men, only hardens Ahaz, and the witnesses gather their sharpest words around the chronicler's own exclamation, "this is that king Ahaz." The reformed John Gill states the paradox: in the time of his distress the king trespassed yet more against the LORD, increasing his idolatries in imitation of what he had seen at Damascus, where he met the king of Assyria. Charles Ellicott of the grammatical-historical school fixes the moment — it was "at the time when Tiglath oppressed him," when Ahaz went to Damascus to do homage, probably in reluctant obedience to a peremptory summons, as at 2 Kings 16:10 — and hears in the closing words a deliberate, emphatic pointing of the finger: "he dealt yet more unfaithfully, he, king Ahaz," the notorious apostate singled out and named for lasting infamy.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley lets his indignation loose upon the phrase. "That Ahaz" — that monster and reproach of mankind, that unteachable and incorrigible prince, whom even grievous afflictions made worse, when they commonly make men better; this is he, Wesley says, whose name deserves to be remembered and detested for ever. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry adds his own recoil from the man: this is that king Ahaz, that wretched man; and he draws the general truth the case exhibits — those are wicked and vile indeed who are made worse by their afflictions instead of better, who in their distress trespass yet more, and have their hearts more fully set in them to do evil.

The witnesses do not divide; they close ranks in condemnation. Gill fixes the fact of the deepening idolatry, Ellicott the emphatic naming, Wesley and Henry the moral horror of a man who answered chastisement with rebellion. What all four see is the perversity that runs to the very root of Ahaz's character. The rod of God is meant to drive a sinner home; it drove Ahaz further off. Every blow that should have humbled him he took as a fresh provocation, until his suffering, far from breaking his idolatry, fed it. The chronicler's stark aside — "this is that king Ahaz" — is not a slip of feeling but a set epitaph, marking out a king whose distresses only proved how hopeless was his hardness, and warning every later reader that afflictions carry no saving virtue in themselves: the same fire that melts the wax bakes the clay, and the same troubles that soften a penitent heart can set an impenitent one like flint.
23:
The depth of Ahaz's folly is laid bare as he offers sacrifice to the gods of the very people who had beaten him, and the witnesses divide sharply over how the strange clause "which smote him" is to be read. The reformed John Gill recoils from taking the words at face value: that a king of Judah should worship the idols that had hurt him, thinking thereby to buy their favour, is monstrous stupidity; rather, he urges, the sense must be that Ahaz sacrificed to the gods of the men of Damascus who smote him, for the Spirit of God would never ascribe his defeat to idols, however Ahaz in his blindness might. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the same difficulty by a textual road. He reports Mr. Hallet's surprise that the sacred historian himself should seem to say the gods of Damascus had smitten Ahaz, when Scripture everywhere treats the idols as nothing; and he follows the older Hebrew copies behind the Greek, which read, "And King Ahaz said, I will seek to the gods of Damascus which have smitten me" — making the mad assertion Ahaz's own speech, not the writer's judgment.

The grammatical-historical voices keep the received text and read it otherwise. Keil and Delitzsch correct the tense: the participle is not pluperfect, "who had smitten him," as though Ahaz turned to the Syrian gods after the war, but present, "who smite him" — he sacrificed to them while the Syrians were still inflicting their defeats, in the vain hope of turning their gods to his side. Charles Ellicott asks the underlying question directly: did the chronicler himself believe those gods had power? The common belief of Israel in that age half-granted it; and there was the further current thought, which Paul repeats, that what the heathen sacrifice they sacrifice to demons, as at 1 Corinthians 10:20 and Deuteronomy 32:17. Ellicott adds the verse's grim close: those very gods "were the ruin of him, and of all Israel" — the props Ahaz leaned on became the thing that made him stumble.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the moral over the whole tangle: no marvel that men's affections and devotions are misplaced when they mistake the author of their trouble and of their help. So the witnesses circle a real disagreement — whether to repoint the clause as Ahaz's own deluded words, or to keep it as the historian's description of the gods the Syrians served — without dissolving the horror they all confess. A king chastened by the living God ran for refuge to the idols of his conquerors, and found in them not rescue but ruin.
24:
Ahaz turns from importing false worship to demolishing the true, and the witnesses trace the desecration of the temple stroke by stroke. The reformed John Gill reads the plainest motive into the deed: Ahaz gathered the vessels of the house of God and cut them in pieces, converting them to his own use, selling them or melting down their gold and silver for money, his own treasures being now exhausted by the Assyrian tribute. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe a more deliberate sacrilege: not content with worshipping strange gods, Ahaz laid violent hands on the sacred vessels and suppressed the temple service itself. The "cutting" they explain from the parallel — he mutilated the artistic furniture of the court, cut the panels from the bases and removed the lavers, and took down the brazen sea from the oxen that bore it, as told at 2 Kings 16:17 — and then he shut the doors of the house of the LORD, to put an end to a worship he now counted superfluous, having set up his own altars at every corner of Jerusalem.

Charles Ellicott sharpens the philology and marks what is peculiar to the chronicler. "Cut in pieces" is literally "trimmed," that is stripped off the metal ornaments; and the shutting of the doors, which Kings does not mention, must mean the doors of the sanctuary itself, not those of the great court, so that by closing them Ahaz suspended every rite that could be performed only within the holy place and the holy of holies. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the duration of that darkness: Ahaz caused the divine worship to be totally suspended, and the doors stood shut until the very beginning of Hezekiah's reign, one of whose first acts was to reopen them and restore the service of God, as at 2 Chronicles 29:3.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill supplies the mercenary motive, Keil and Ellicott the detail of the mutilation and the closing of the sanctuary, Clarke the length of the silence and its glad ending under Hezekiah. Together they show the last stage of the apostasy: the king who had filled the land with strange altars now bolts the doors of the one true house, stripping and breaking its holy vessels and quenching its worship altogether. It is the logical end of a reign that began with molten Baals — not merely to add idols to the LORD, but at last to shut the LORD out. Yet even here the chronicler leaves a seam of hope, for the doors Ahaz closed a better son will open, and the fire he extinguished will burn again.
25:
The apostasy spreads to fill the whole land, and the witnesses read the verse as the outward completion of Ahaz's ruin. The reformed John Gill notes the calculated policy in it: in every several city of Judah Ahaz made high places to burn incense to the gods — the gods of Damascus and other idols — and did so, Gill suggests, to prevent the people from resorting to Jerusalem for worship, since he had shut the temple there. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep close to the verse's own verdict: he made high places in city after city to burn incense to other gods, and thereby provoked to anger the LORD God of his fathers — the God of the covenant, deliberately affronted by a descendant of David who scattered rival shrines through the covenant land.

Charles Ellicott anchors the phrase and the wider picture. "Provoked to anger" echoes the ancient warning of Deuteronomy 32:16, that strange gods provoke the LORD to jealousy; and he compares the multiplied high places with the idolatry already charged earlier in the chapter, reading this closing summary of Ahaz's worship as the counterpart to the further temple-changes he made for fear of the Assyrian. The whole sacrilege, Ellicott judges, went together — stripping the house of God of everything of value to satisfy the rapacious conqueror, and studding the land with altars to the gods that conqueror served.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the verse into its warning. The progress of wickedness and misery is often rapid, he observes; and it is an awful thing to reflect upon a sinner being driven away in his wickedness into the eternal world. Ahaz is that sinner drawn to the life: each stage of his reign steeper than the last, from molten images to child-sacrifice, from foreign gods to the shut temple, and now to a whole kingdom sown with idolatry — a headlong descent broken only by death. The witnesses do not divide. Gill exposes the crafty design of the country shrines, Keil and Ellicott the affront to the covenant God, Henry the terror of a life hurrying unrepentant to its account. Together they close the record of Ahaz's deeds where it must close, at the point of maximum provocation: a king who had turned every city of Judah into a place of false incense, and so filled up, to its last measure, the anger of the God of his fathers.
26:
The record of the reign draws toward its close with the customary appeal to the fuller annals, and the witnesses read even this dry formula for what it reveals of the chronicler's method. The reformed John Gill treats the notice as matter already handled, pointing the reader on to the parallel record for the rest of Ahaz's acts and referring the details elsewhere rather than repeating them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks that the chronicler has varied his usual closing formula here, writing "the rest of his acts, and of all his ways, first and last," where the set phrase runs otherwise — the same variation he had noted at the like notices of earlier kings, as at 2 Chronicles 25:26 and 2 Chronicles 26:7, and as the parallel stands at 2 Kings 16:19. The acts and ways alike are said to be written in the book of the kings of Judah and Israel, the common source to which the sacred writer defers for the political detail he does not stop to relate.

Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, take the verse as the formal head of the reign's ending, the notice that gathers up all that remains of Ahaz's history before the account turns to his death and burial. What the witnesses register between them is the deliberate reticence of the chronicler. He has not written a full chronicle of Ahaz's wars and works — those lie in the royal annals, open to any who would consult them — but has selected, all through the chapter, the events that most conspicuously display the hand of God upon an apostate king, subordinating the historical to the didactic throughout. The formula is his way of acknowledging that much is left untold, and of directing the curious to the larger record, while he keeps his own narrative fixed on the lesson he means to teach.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill defers to the parallel, Ellicott weighs the varied wording and names the source, Keil fixes the verse as the seam where the reign is wound up. Together they show the chronicler at his editor's work, taking over the older annals where they serve his purpose and passing lightly over the rest — not the historian of Ahaz for Ahaz's sake, but a preacher of providence who tells just so much of a wicked reign as will teach the reader to fear the God that reign defied. The "rest of his acts" are dismissed in a phrase; the meaning of them has filled the chapter.
27:
The reign ends as it deserved, in a burial marked by a pointed dishonour, and the witnesses read the death-notice for its studied withholding of a king's due. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch observe that Ahaz indeed slept with his fathers and was buried in the city, in Jerusalem, as the parallel records at 2 Kings 16:20; but he was not laid in the sepulchres of the kings. Since "Israel" here bears its pregnant sense, the people of God, the very phrasing — "in the city, in Jerusalem," and not "with David" — seems purposely chosen to intimate that Ahaz, because in life he had not walked like his ancestor David, was in death denied a place among the royal dead. Charles Ellicott marks the same clause as peculiar to the chronicler, wanting in Kings, and sets it beside the like refusals recorded of earlier evil kings, as at 2 Chronicles 21:20. He weighs and rejects the critic Thenius, who would trace the statement either to a mere mistake or to a later zeal for the Law: why not, Ellicott asks, to a genuine written authority the chronicler had before him?

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke attends to the title "the kings of Israel," where Judah is meant. It is a common thing, he notes, for the writer of this book to put Israel for Judah, still regarding the two as one people because sprung from one stock; the versions and manuscripts agree with the Hebrew, and the interpretation is plain enough that none need mistake it.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott expose the deliberate slight in the burial, Clarke settles the familiar naming, and all pass on to the single bright word with which the chapter shuts — that Hezekiah his son reigned in his stead. The contrast is left to speak for itself. Ahaz, who shut the doors of the temple and burned his children in the valley and studded Judah with strange altars, is carried to a grave outside the honoured tombs of the house of David, refused in death the fellowship of the kings he had disgraced; and the throne he had so nearly ruined passes to a son who will open what his father closed. The chronicler ends the wicked reign on a note of judgment tempered by promise: the apostate is buried in dishonour, but the line of David is not extinguished, and a reformer already stands at the door.
